principle_name: Personalize the Opening to Earn a Stranger's First Few Seconds
author: Alex Hormozi
when_to_use: In the opening line of any cold call, cold email, or LinkedIn message to a prospect who has never interacted with the company before.
when_not_to_use: When reaching out to a warm contact or existing relationship — personalization research is unnecessary overhead there since trust already exists.
principle: A cold message that references one or two specific, real details about the recipient (their company, a recent project, a shared connection) earns far more attention than a generic opener, because it signals the message was not mass-blasted and briefly mimics a warm introduction.
recommended_action: Spend two to three minutes researching each target account (recent expansion, a specific product line, a LinkedIn post, a mutual connection) before sending the first outreach message, and open with that detail rather than a generic pitch.
example: Opening a cold email to an OEM's vendor development contact with a specific reference to their recent plant expansion or a principle_named product line, rather than 'We are a precision machining supplier.'
counter_example: Sending a templated cold email that could be sent unchanged to any company in the industry.
motm_application: Supports MOTM-K06/K15 prospecting and OEM account-entry outreach — reinforces that the Customer Website Analyzer's extracted facts (products, capabilities, industries) should be woven into the opening line of outreach messages, not just used for internal context.

principle_name: Lead with Concrete Value Before Asking for Anything
author: Alex Hormozi
when_to_use: When the first outreach message currently asks for a meeting or call before offering anything of tangible value to the recipient.
when_not_to_use: When the relationship is already warm, or when the ask itself (e.g. a specific technical proposal already requested) is what the recipient wants.
principle: Strangers give very little benefit of the doubt and need a concrete, upfront reason to respond; a vague ask (e.g. 'let's hop on a call') converts far worse than an offer that gives something useful immediately, such as a capability assessment, a sample, or specific relevant insight.
recommended_action: Replace generic meeting requests in cold outreach with a specific, low-effort value offer — e.g. a free feasibility check on a part drawing, a capability comparison, or a relevant case reference — before asking for time.
example: Instead of 'Can we schedule a call to discuss your sourcing needs,' offer 'Send us your manifold block drawing and we'll return a DFM feasibility note within 48 hours, no obligation.'
counter_example: A first cold email that only introduces the company and asks for 15 minutes of the prospect's time.
motm_application: Directly relevant to MOTM Sales Engineer mode account-entry outreach (MOTM-K15) — the 'first ask' in cold outreach to OEM/technical buyers should be reframed as a value offer rather than a meeting request.

principle_name: Multiple Channels and Multiple Attempts Beat a Single Well-Crafted Message
author: Alex Hormozi
when_to_use: When a single outreach attempt (one email, one call) has gone unanswered and the natural instinct is to move on to a different prospect.
when_not_to_use: When the contact has explicitly asked not to be contacted again, or when repeated outreach would violate an account's stated preference.
principle: A non-response usually reflects timing or attention, not disinterest — trying a different channel (call after an unanswered email, a message after an unanswered call) both increases the chance of being seen and signals seriousness, since most people only try once before giving up.
recommended_action: Sequence outreach across at least two to three channels (e.g. email, then phone, then LinkedIn) rather than repeating the same channel, and explicitly reference the earlier attempt ('following up on my email from Tuesday').
example: Following an unanswered email to a purchase manager with a phone call referencing the email, rather than sending a second, near-identical email.
counter_example: Sending three emails in a row with no response and then abandoning the account.
motm_application: Reinforces MOTM-K12 (Follow-Up Framework) with a channel-diversity angle that complements POS-0001's 'five touches' principle from The Psychology of Selling — together they suggest both quantity and channel variety matter for follow-up.

principle_name: Circumstances Change — Re-Contact Cold Lists After a Waiting Period
author: Alex Hormozi
when_to_use: When a prospect list has gone cold after an initial outreach sequence, and the accounts have not been actively pursued again.
when_not_to_use: When the prospect has given a firm, permanent no (e.g. a signed long-term exclusive contract elsewhere) rather than simply 'not now.'
principle: A prospect who was uninterested at first contact may become a strong lead later purely because their circumstances changed (a new project, a supplier issue, a budget cycle) — the same list re-approached months later can produce new engaged leads without any new list-building effort.
recommended_action: Maintain the outreach list even after an unsuccessful first sequence, and schedule a re-approach after a defined waiting period (e.g. one or two quarters) rather than discarding non-responsive accounts permanently.
example: An OEM that showed no interest six months ago due to a new-vendor freeze may be worth re-approaching after their fiscal year resets.
counter_example: Deleting an account from the pipeline permanently after one unsuccessful outreach sequence.
motm_application: Supports MOTM-K16 (Distributor Development) and account revival scenarios (`revival` sales stage) — gives a concrete rationale and cadence for re-engaging accounts that previously went cold.

principle_name: Track Outreach Metrics to Diagnose Where the Funnel Is Actually Failing
author: Alex Hormozi
when_to_use: When a sales manager or rep is unsure why an outreach campaign is underperforming and is tempted to change everything at once.
when_not_to_use: Not applicable to a single one-off outreach attempt — this principle applies to a running outreach process with enough volume to measure.
principle: Breaking outreach into discrete, measurable stages (contacted -> responded -> engaged -> converted) makes it possible to identify exactly which stage is underperforming, rather than guessing at the cause of poor results; without this breakdown, teams tend to declare 'outreach doesn't work' without knowing which step actually failed.
recommended_action: Track and review conversion rates at each discrete stage of outreach (contact rate, response rate, meeting-booked rate, meeting-to-opportunity rate) rather than only tracking overall deals won.
example: Discovering that 90% of a rep's emails are opened but only 2% get a reply points to a messaging problem, not a targeting or list-quality problem.
counter_example: Concluding 'cold outreach isn't working for us' after a few weeks without ever measuring open, response, or meeting-booked rates separately.
motm_application: Supports the observability principles in the MOTM AI Sales Director brief (Section 65) and MOTM-K06 (Sales Process) — reinforces stage-level metric tracking for BD prospecting activity, feeding failure analysis (Section 64 of the brief).
